title: Chapter XIII

teacherSummary.text: Mr. Bennet reads a letter from Mr. Collins, the clergyman cousin who will inherit Longbourn. Collins arrives, pompous and obsequious, praising his patroness Lady Catherine de Bourgh.

discussionQuestions: What words would you use for Collins's letter, and why?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XIII,” how does Austen show an absurd cousin's letter? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XIII develops the idea of an absurd cousin's letter. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XIII to complicate the reader's understanding of an absurd cousin's letter. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of an absurd cousin's letter responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of an absurd cousin's letter. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: “It certainly is a most iniquitous affair,” said Mr. Bennet, “and nothing can clear Mr. Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn. But if you will listen to his letter, you may perhaps be a little softened by his manner of expressing himself.”

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood
annotationFocus.lookFor: word choices that reveal the narrator's attitude or the scene's feeling

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: What words would you use for Collins's letter, and why? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include inheriting, asperity, complimented, atonement, injuring. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: (Law) To take by descent from an ancestor.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Clergymen often depended on wealthy patrons for their livings. Now, why does this chapter matter? Collins is a comic masterpiece who satirizes both sycophancy and the church's dependence on rank. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
segments.passage: “It certainly is a most iniquitous affair,” said Mr. Bennet, “and nothing can clear Mr. Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn. But if you will listen to his letter, you may perhaps be a little softened by his manner of expressing himself.”
